core: Literary texts, cultural interpretation and identity
Language structure, meaning and multilingual processing
Cultural history, visual culture and European/international contexts
Humanities research, philosophical interpretation and academic expression
questions: How do texts and images construct cultural identity?
How do language structure and multilingualism shape meaning?
How do historical and European contexts shape cultural interpretation?

trace: Practical literary interpretation, narrative form, close reading and critical sources directly implement the literary-analysis discipline; no French corpus is implied.
Actual painting analysis, artistic movements and social/historical contextualisation directly support visual-cultural interpretation. It is a Western survey, not a French art/architecture sequence.
Neural and psychological foundations support the actual Psycholinguistics course; they do not supply French grammar or language proficiency.

International-relations theories, historical/colonial cases and country-position research provide a specific institutional/geopolitical context for France and international-organisation interests; a French country project is not guaranteed.
Grammar, discourse, cognition, narration and text worlds connect linguistic choices to literary interpretation through actual stylistic analysis.
Comparative close reading of literary works and recurring themes supplies sustained literary study without claiming a French-language canon.
Actual language acquisition, bilingualism and comprehension/production inquiry directly support the multilingual-language element; no French-specific linguistic sequence is claimed.
Modern nationalism, ideologies, industrialisation and world wars provide specific historical context for interpreting modern European cultural questions, without a French-specialist sequence.
Film form, expressionism, adaptation and independent interpretation provide concrete film/media analytical methods; not a complete French film-history sequence.
Print, optical and sound media as cultural artifacts supply material-historical methods for studying mediated culture, not specifically French media content.
Classical theories including Marx and Weber, modernity and stratification supply specific social-theoretical tools for interpreting culture and historical change.
Interviews, textual/documentary and visual analysis, coding, reflexivity and research ethics provide concrete empirical humanities/cultural-research complements.
Life narratives, memory, identity and cultural positioning are analysed through close reading and comparative research; it is not a French study-abroad replacement.
Philosophical arguments about mind, identity, experience and mind–body relations complement the explicit language/brain and reflective humanities inquiry.
Documentary analysis, historical/ethical representation, interviewing and short-film research develop concrete cultural analysis and research practice.
Adaptation theory, medium specificity, intertextuality and text/film research directly extend literary and cultural interpretation.
Comparative myth, narrative transmission and literary theory provide a comparative literary contribution, not French myth/corpus teaching.
Actual European institutions, integration and policy-document research provide a specific complement to the evidenced France/Europe question; no French political history course is invented.
Critical theory, modernity, phenomenology and cultural/social interpretation provide specific theoretical perspectives for interpreting cultural identity and power.
Actual ethical arguments and close reading provide philosophical inquiry; this is not equated with the external Philosophy of Culture syllabus.
Humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic interpretation is applied in literary research, directly sustaining the humanities core.
Poetic form, sound, voice, performance and research-grounded creative work directly supply literary/communicative inquiry; no French-language creative-writing equivalence.

Description-only evidence: disciplinary historiography, meaning, identity and texts by Foucault and Derrida sustain critical visual/intellectual inquiry. No detailed outline, French canon or French-language teaching is inferred.

alternatives.label: Literature, language and visual-cultural interpretation
alternatives.concept: A programme interpreting literary texts, language, images and cultural identities through close reading, stylistics, psycholinguistics, film and art analysis. Historical, social-theoretical, philosophical and international inquiry provide specific contexts. This is broader humanities study rather than a French-language or francophone regional specialisation.
alternatives.labelReason: Sustained literary, language and visual-cultural study is present in the actual courses; no French Studies or advanced-French label is asserted.
progression: Covered offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked against current workbook; PPD is in year one and the psychology gateway precedes Psycholinguistics.

candidates.label: French–Dutch legal and administrative translation
candidates.reason: Actual Private Law includes France in comparative property/tort/contract inquiry and IRAC/legal research, but requires the law gateway and supplies neither French–Dutch translation practice nor administrative/legal bilingual text analysis. Stylistics and creative writing add language/literary inquiry without that translation substance. These contributions cannot sustain a distinct full translation programme; the objection concerns taught content, not professional translator entitlement.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the French specialisation of Romance Languages and Cultures. Within its restricted final-year pair and thesis options, the first-listed Research Seminar/Administrative Translation pair and Cultural Studies thesis are retained independently of UCR fit.

selection.assessment: One meaningful broader confirmed-core response passes. The eligible translation direction lacks sustained actual bilingual/legal-translation teaching. Multilingualism is a core/supporting subject here, not an additional eligible stand-alone cognitive generator; career and illustration rows do not create alternatives.

blocks: Both analyse language and texts. UCR teaches stylistic grammar, discourse, narration and meaning in English/comparative texts; it does not establish identical French-text analysis or language proficiency.
Both address multilingualism, language and the brain. UCR teaches acquisition, bilingual processing and language comprehension/production; no identical French-specific syllabus is certified.

notes.text: UCR offers broader literary, language and visual-cultural inquiry. It does not provide advanced French proficiency, a francophone literary/history and French-linguistics sequence, French–Dutch translation training or the integrated French professional/internship experience.

audience.programmeDescription: Study French language, literature and culture, including linguistics, French-speaking societies and the history of France. The degree develops advanced spoken and written French and academic research skills.
audience.comparisonExplanation: A broader UCR programme in literary, language and visual-cultural interpretation meaningfully addresses the confirmed scholarly core, without reproducing French-specialist formation or certifying the unresolved complete pathway. The unknown required 15 EC are excluded. UCR supplies broader analytical study and does not teach advanced French, a francophone specialist sequence or French–Dutch translation. Formal progression and mobility arrangements are not certified.

curriculum.limitation: The nominal degree is 180 EC. The current regulations repeat three 5-EC courses in years one and two; 165 distinct EC are documented. The missing 15 EC and their ordinary cohort allocation remain unresolved.

comparisonScope.label: Qualified academic-core comparison
comparisonScope.assessed: Confirmed literary/textual, linguistic/multilingual, cultural and research study, together with separately identified restricted Arts packages and genuine broadening space: 165 distinct documented EC.
comparisonScope.excluded: The unidentified 15 EC and their cohort replacement/rotation allocation; any dependent specialist or mobility culmination; certification of a complete ordinary external pathway.

acceptance.claim: A broader UCR programme in literary, language and visual-cultural interpretation meaningfully addresses the confirmed scholarly core, without reproducing French-specialist formation or certifying the unresolved complete pathway.
acceptance.targetContext: Exact French specialisation of Radboud Romance Languages and Cultures, CROHO56074, ordinary 2026–2027 entry. Current OER and neutral first-listed within-specialisation choices; no Spanish, old-cohort or future prospectus curriculum substituted.
acceptance.challengeMethod: Separately identified source-first second pass by the same AI against official OER, substantive programme evidence and current UCR content. No independent human or separate-agent review.

uncertainties.fact: The nominal degree is 180 EC. The current regulations repeat three 5-EC courses in years one and two; 165 distinct EC are documented. The missing 15 EC and their ordinary cohort allocation remain unresolved.

adverseResolutions.resolution: The missing15 EC add specialist French literary/cultural study, linguistic analysis or translation in the early/middle years.
adverseResolutions.effectOnClaim: The complete specialist weighting and exact pathway may change. The independently confirmed text/identity/memory/culture and language inquiry remains; no unidentified component or full specialist sequence is compared.
